It has also been said that *ma* in His saying ﴿and what you are promised﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾, so the pronoun refers back to *ma*.

Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿like that you speak﴾. The majority read *mithla* with the accusative (*nasb*), on the presumption of "like your speech", with *ma* being superfluous (*za'idah*). Some of the Kufans said this, that it is accusative by the removal of the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*).

al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: it may be in the accusative as an emphatic (*tawkid*), that is: it is truly true, like your speech.

al-Mazini said: *mithl* together with *ma* has the status of a single word, and so it is built on the fatha.

Sibawayh said: it is indeclinable (*mabni*) because it is annexed to something that is not fully declinable. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and al-A'mash read *mithlu* with the nominative, as an adjective (*sifah*) of *haqq*, because *mithl* is indefinite, and even when annexed it does not become definite, like *ghayr*.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the view of al-Mazini, and said: a similar example is the saying of Humayd:

*Woe to whoever does not know what they are, woe indeed!*

Here *waylan* is built with *ma* and is not given tanwin. The meaning of the verse is a comparison of the certainty of what Allah has informed about with the certainty of human speech and existence. This is like your saying: "it is true, as you are here", and "it is true, as you are speaking." The meaning is that it is true in its truthfulness and existence, as what you know by necessity.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar the like of this.

Ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also regarding the verse: "they used to sleep only little."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, transmitted from Anas regarding the verse: "they used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha'."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar regarding ﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾: "they pray."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾: "other than the zakat, by which one maintains kinship, or hosts a guest, or helps a deprived person."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "The beggar (*sa'il*) is the one who asks people, and the deprived (*mahrum*) is the one who has no share of the spoils (*fay'*) of the Muslims."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "The deprived is the one who is in want (*muharif*), who seeks the world and it turns away from him, and who does not ask people. So Allah commanded the believers to support him."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'A'ishah regarding the verse: "He is the one in want, whose livelihood hardly becomes easy for him."

al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Fatimah bint Qays that she asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this verse, and he said: "Indeed, in wealth there is a right other than the zakat," and he recited this verse: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west…﴾ up to His saying ﴿and [gives wealth] to the slaves, and establishes prayer and gives zakat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾: "the path of defecation and urination."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 51, verse 1–23 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Dhariyat was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿By the winds that scatter dust, scattering﴾. It is said: dharat al-rih al-turab tadhruhu dharwan (the wind scattered the dust), and adhrat tudhriihi dharyan. He, glorified is He, swore by the winds that scatter the dust. The accusative of "dharwan" is as a verbal noun (masdar), and the governing element in it is the active participle, while the object is omitted.

Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read the "ta'" of (al-Dhariyat) as assimilated into the "dhal" of (dharwan). The rest read without assimilation.

It was said: the one sworn by is implied, and it is the Lord of the winds and what follows them; but the first (view) is more preferable.

﴿And by those that bear a load﴾. They are the clouds, which carry water as the four-legged animals carry a load. The accusative of (wiqran) is as its being an object, as it is said: "So-and-so carried a heavy bag." The majority read (wiqran) with a kasra on the waw, as the name of what is carried, i.e., what is borne. It was read with a fatha on it, as a verbal noun, with the governing element being the active participle, or by calling the carried thing by the verbal noun for emphasis.

﴿And by those that glide with ease﴾. They are the ships that run on the sea with the winds, gliding easily.

The accusative of (yusran) is as a verbal noun, or an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or as a circumstantial state: i.e., gliding with ease.

It was said: they are the winds. It was said: the clouds. The first is more preferable.

Al-yusr: ease in everything.

﴿And by those that distribute by command﴾. They are the angels who distribute the affairs.

Al-Farra' said: they bring different commands: Jibril with severity, Mika'il with mercy, and the Angel of Death brings death. It was said: they bring different commands of drought, fertility, rain, death, and events.

It was said: they are the clouds through which Allah distributes the affairs of His servants. It was said: the intended meaning of the dhariyat, the hamilat, the jariyat, and the muqassimat is the winds, for they are described by all of that: they scatter dust, carry clouds, run through the air, and distribute rains. But this is very weak.

The accusative of (amran) is as the object; it was said: as a state, i.e., commanded. The first is more preferable.

﴿Indeed what you are promised is true﴾. This is the answer to the oath: i.e., what you are promised of reward and punishment will certainly come about.

(Ma) may be a relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun, or a verbal (masdariyya) particle.

The reason for singling out these matters for oaths is that they are wondrous matters contrary to the usual course; so whoever is able to do these is able to resurrect, which is what is promised.

﴿And by the heaven with its paths﴾. The majority read (al-hubuk) with a damma on the ha' and the ba'. It was read with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the ba', and with a kasra on the ha' and a fatha on the ba', and with a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the ba'.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: these are dialects. The intended "heaven" here is the well-known one. It was said: the intended meaning is the clouds; but the first is more preferable.

The commentators differed in the interpretation of (al-hubuk). Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said: the meaning is "possessing a well-proportioned, beautiful creation."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: everything you have made firm and done well, you have "habakta" and "ihtabakta" it.

al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "possessing adornment."

It is also narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "possessing stars."

al-Dahhak said: "possessing paths," and al-Farra' said likewise. It is said of what you see in water and sand when the wind touches it: hubuk.

Al-Farra' said: al-hibk with a kasra: everything like sand when still wind passes over it, and water when wind passes over it. A coat of iron is also called hubuk, and from it is the poet's saying:

"As if the weavers had draped it with a carpet, in whose weaving are hibak (lines)."

i.e., paths.

It was said: al-habk means strength, and the meaning is: "and by the heaven possessing strength." A firmly made one (mahbuk) is a strongly created one, of a horse or other, and from it is the poet's saying:

"He has begun to carry me on his nose, a swift one with firm flanks, well-built and firmly made."

Another said:

"Religion has become disordered, so I prepared for it one with a high withers and a firmly knit shoulder-blade."

Al-Wahidi, after relating the first opinion, said: this is the view of most of them.

﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. This is the answer to the oath by the heaven possessing paths: i.e., indeed you, O people of Makkah, are in a discordant, contradictory saying about Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace: some of you say he is a poet, some of you say he is a sorcerer, and some of you say he is a madman.

The reason for specifying the oath by the heaven described by that attribute is the comparison of their sayings in their divergence to the divergence of the heaven's paths. The use of hubuk for paths is what the lexicographers hold, although most commentators differ from it.

Moreover, those sayings about the interpretation of hubuk may return to this, by saying that what is in the heaven of paths may be a cause of greater beauty, evenness of creation, the existence of adornment in it, and greater strength for it.

It was said: the intended meaning of their being "in a discordant saying" is that some of them deny the Resurrection and some doubt it. It was said: their acknowledging that Allah is their Creator while worshipping idols.

﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾. That is: he is turned away from belief in the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and from what he brought, or from the truth, which is the Resurrection and monotheism, whoever is turned away.

It was said: whoever Allah has turned away from that discord by protection and success is turned away from it. It is said: afakahu yafakuhu ifkan: i.e., he turned him from a thing and diverted him from it, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: have you come to us to turn us away?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22]. Mujahid said: "yu'fan 'anhu man ufin" (he is deprived of sense whoever is deprived of sense); al-afn is corruption of the intellect. It was said: "yuhram-hu man hurim" (he is deprived of it whoever is deprived).

Qutrub said: "yujda' 'anhu man judi'" (he is cut off from it whoever is cut off).

al-Yazidi said: "yudfa' 'anhu man dufi'" (he is repelled from it whoever is repelled).

﴿Slain are the conjecturers﴾. This is a curse upon them.

al-Wahidi related from the commentators all together that the meaning is: "the liars are cursed."

Ibn al-Anbari said: qatl, when reported about Allah, has the meaning of cursing, because whomever Allah curses is like one who has been slain and destroyed.

al-Farra' said: the meaning of qutila is: "cursed."

Al-kharrasun: the liars who guess about what they do not know, so they say: Muhammad is a madman, a liar, a poet, a sorcerer.

al-Zajjaj said: al-kharrasun are the liars, and al-kharS is estimating what is on the palm trees of ripe dates as dates; al-kharrasu is the one who estimates them, and that is not what is meant here.

Then He said: ﴿Who are in heedlessness, inattentive﴾. That is: in negligence and the blindness of ignorance concerning the affairs of the Hereafter. The meaning of (sahun) is: frivolous, heedless. Sahw is negligence of a thing and its departure from the heart. The origin of ghamrah is what covers and overspreads a thing, and from it are the pangs (ghamarat) of death.

﴿They ask: when is the Day of Judgment?﴾. That is: they say when the Day of Recompense is, in denial and mockery.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about that day, saying: ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾. That is: they will be burned and punished. It is said: fatantu al-dhahab: when you burn it to test it, and the origin of fitnah is testing.

'Ikrimah said: Do you not see that when gold is put into fire it is said: it was fatana (tested)?

The accusative of (yawma) is governed by an implied element: i.e., the requital is on the day they are over the Fire. It may be a substitute for (yawm al-din), and the fatha is for construction because it is attached to a clause. It was said: it is accusative by the implied "I mean."

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (yawmu) with a damma as a substitute for (yawm al-din).

The clause ﴿Taste your fitnah﴾ is by implied speech: i.e., it will be said to them: taste your punishment; said by Ibn Zayd. Mujahid said: your burning. al-Farra' preferred the first.

The clause ﴿This is what you used to seek to hasten﴾ is part of what is quoted by the saying: i.e., this is what you used to seek to hasten, in mockery from you. It was said: it is a substitute for "your fitnah".

﴿Indeed the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾. When He, glorified is He, mentioned the state of the people of the Fire, He mentioned the state of the people of Paradise: i.e., they will be in orchards in which there are flowing springs, whose description the describers cannot reach.

﴿Receiving what their Lord has given them﴾. That is: accepting what their Lord has given them of good and honor. The clause ﴿Indeed they were before that doers of good﴾ is a reason for what precedes it: i.e., because they were in the world doers of good in their righteous deeds, by doing what they were commanded and abandoning what they were forbidden.

Then He explained their goodness, which He described them with, saying: ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾. Al-huju': sleep at night, not by day. The meaning: they used to sleep little of the night. (Ma) is superfluous, and it may be a verbal (masdariyya) particle or a relative pronoun: i.e., they were little of the night in their sleep, or in what they slept. From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"The helmet has pressed upon my head, so I do not taste sleep except a light doze."

Al-tuhja': a little of sleep. From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

"Does the caller and the hearer of Rayhanah stir me, and my companions in slumber?"

It was said: (ma) is negative, i.e., they did not sleep a little of the night, let alone much of it; and this is very weak.

This is the view of those who say the meaning is that their number was small.

Then He began: ﴿They sleep not﴾, and Ibn al-Anbari said so, and it is weaker than what precedes it.

Qatadah said in the interpretation of this verse: they used to pray between the two evening prayers; Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Wahb said likewise.

﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾. That is: they ask Allah, glorified is He, in the times of dawn to forgive their sins.

al-Hasan said: they extended the prayer to the dawns, then took up seeking forgiveness at the dawns.

al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Mujahid said: they pray at the dawns, because their prayer is a request from them for forgiveness.

al-Dahhak said: it is the Fajr prayer.

Then He mentioned their charities, saying: ﴿And in their wealth is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾. That is: they place in their wealth, on themselves, a right for the beggar and the deprived, seeking nearness to Allah, mighty and majestic.

Muhammad ibn Sirin and Qatadah said: the right here is the obligatory zakah. The first is more preferable, so it is taken to mean voluntary charity, the maintenance of kinship, and hospitality to guests, because the surah is Meccan, and zakah was not made obligatory except in Madinah. It will come in Surat Sa'ala Sa'il: ﴿In their wealth is a known right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 24–25], with the addition of "known." The beggar is the one who asks people because of his poverty.

It is differed concerning the interpretation of the deprived. It was said: he is the one who abstains from asking until people think him rich, so they do not give to him; this is the view of Qatadah and al-Zuhri.

al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: he is the one who has no share in the spoils and from whom nothing from the fay' is paid. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is the one whose fruit, crop or livestock has been struck. al-Qurtubi said: he is the one whom a calamity has struck. It was said: he who does not earn; it was said: he who does not find a sufficiency to suffice him; it was said: he who seeks the world and it turns away from him; it was said: he is the owned one; it was said: the dog; it was said: other than that.

al-Sha'bi said: For me today there are seventy years since I reached puberty, asking about the deprived, and I am today no more knowledgeable about it than I was then. What should be relied upon is what the linguistic meaning indicates: al-mahrum in the language is the prevented, from hirman, which is prevention. It therefore includes whoever is deprived of provision from the root, whoever has had his wealth struck by a calamity that destroyed it, whoever is deprived of a gift, and whoever is deprived of charity because of his abstinence.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the signs He has set up, indicating His oneness and the truth of His promise and threat, saying: ﴿And in the earth are signs for the certain﴾. That is: clear proofs and manifest indications, from the mountains, the land, the sea, the trees, the rivers, and the fruits; and in them are traces of destruction for the disbelieving nations who denied what the messengers of Allah brought and called them to. He singled out those certain of Allah because they are the ones who acknowledge that and reflect upon it, so they benefit from it.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 51, verses 1–23 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ That is: in yourselves there are signs that point to the Oneness of Allah and to the truth of what the messengers brought. He created them as a drop (*nutfah*), then a clinging clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then bones, until He breathes the spirit (*ruh*) into them. After that their forms, colours, natures and tongues differ. Then the very creation of them in this wondrous state, of flesh, blood, bone, limbs, senses, passages, and channels, is itself a sign. The meaning of ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ is: will you not look with the eye of insight, so that you may infer from this the Creator, the Provider, who alone is worthy of divinity, that He has no partner, no equal and no rival, that His promise is true, that His word is true, and that what His messengers have brought you is the truth about which there is no doubt and against which no doubt can prevail. It has also been said that by "the selves" (*anfus*) is meant the spirits (*arwah*), that is: in your souls, through which you live, there are signs.

﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾: that is, the cause of your provision, which is rain, for it is the cause of sustenance.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: "Provision here means what descends from the heaven, of rain and snow."

It has also been said that by "the heaven" is meant the clouds, that is: in the clouds is your provision. It has been said that by "the heaven" is meant rain, and it was called "heaven" because it descends from its direction. From this is the saying of the poet:

*When the sky descends upon the land of a people,*
*we graze upon it, even if they are angry.*

Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning is "and upon the Lord of the heaven is your provision," and a parallel to this is ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud: 6], but this is far-fetched.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: that is, with Allah in the heaven is your provision.

It has also been said that the meaning is: in the heaven is the decree of your provision.

The majority read *rizqukum* in the singular, while Ya'qub, Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read *arzaqukum* in the plural.

﴿And what you are promised﴾: of Paradise and Hellfire, as said by Mujahid. 'Ata' said: of reward and punishment. al-Kalbi said: of good and evil. Ibn Sirin said: what you are promised of the matter of the Hour. al-Rabi' also said this.

The preferable reading is to take it in the sense that is more general than all these opinions, for the recompense of deeds is written in the heaven, the decree and destiny descend from it, and Paradise and Hellfire are in it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, swore by Himself, saying: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾, that is, what I inform you of in these verses.

al-Zajjaj said: it is what He mentioned of the matter of provision and the signs.

al-Kalbi said: it means what was related in the Book.

Muqatil said: it means the matter of the Hour.

It has also been said that *ma* in His saying ﴿and what you are promised﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾, so the pronoun refers back to *ma*.

Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿like that you speak﴾. The majority read *mithla* with the accusative (*nasb*), on the presumption of "like your speech", with *ma* being superfluous (*za'idah*). Some of the Kufans said this, that it is accusative by the removal of the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*).

al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: it may be in the accusative as an emphatic (*tawkid*), that is: it is truly true, like your speech.

al-Mazini said: *mithl* together with *ma* has the status of a single word, and so it is built on the fatha.

Sibawayh said: it is indeclinable (*mabni*) because it is annexed to something that is not fully declinable. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and al-A'mash read *mithlu* with the nominative, as an adjective (*sifah*) of *haqq*, because *mithl* is indefinite, and even when annexed it does not become definite, like *ghayr*.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the view of al-Mazini, and said: a similar example is the saying of Humayd:

*Woe to whoever does not know what they are, woe indeed!*

Here *waylan* is built with *ma* and is not given tanwin. The meaning of the verse is a comparison of the certainty of what Allah has informed about with the certainty of human speech and existence. This is like your saying: "it is true, as you are here", and "it is true, as you are speaking." The meaning is that it is true in its truthfulness and existence, as what you know by necessity.

[p. 1406]

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, from various chains, transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His saying ﴿By those that scatter with dispersal﴾: "the winds." ﴿And those that carry a load﴾: "the clouds." ﴿And those that glide with ease﴾: "the ships." ﴿And those that distribute by command﴾: "the angels."

al-Bazzar, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab the like of this, and traced it back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In its chain is Abu Bakr ibn Sabrah, who is weak in narration (*layyin al-hadith*), and Sa'id ibn Sallam, who is not among the people of hadith. So said al-Bazzar.

Ibn Kathir said: this hadith is weak in its attribution to the Prophet, and the closest thing to it is that it is a statement of 'Umar (*mawquf*).

al-Firyabi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas the like of the statement of 'Ali.

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿By the heaven of the intricate paths﴾: "its beauty and its evenness."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* transmitted from him regarding the verse: "possessing splendour and beauty, and its construction is like the hail, interlocked."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar the like of this.

Ibn Mani' transmitted from 'Ali: "it is the seventh heaven."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾: "It is led astray from it, whoever is led astray."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also ﴿Destroyed are the liars﴾: "Cursed are the doubters."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "They are the soothsayers." ﴿Who are in heedlessness, inattentive﴾: "in negligence, playing."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "Heedlessness (*ghamrah*) is disbelief and doubt."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "In their misguidance they keep wandering." And regarding His saying ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾: "they will be punished."

These same transmitters also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Taking what their Lord has given them﴾: "the obligations (*fara'id*)." ﴿Indeed they were before that doers of good﴾: "before the obligations were revealed, they used to act."

These, together with al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat*, transmitted from him also regarding ﴿They used to sleep little of the night﴾: "there was not a night that came upon them in which they slept until morning, except that they prayed during it."

Ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also regarding the verse: "they used to sleep only little."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, transmitted from Anas regarding the verse: "they used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha'."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar regarding ﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾: "they pray."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾: "other than the zakat, by which one maintains kinship, or hosts a guest, or helps a deprived person."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "The beggar (*sa'il*) is the one who asks people, and the deprived (*mahrum*) is the one who has no share of the spoils (*fay'*) of the Muslims."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "The deprived is the one who is in want (*muharif*), who seeks the world and it turns away from him, and who does not ask people. So Allah commanded the believers to support him."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'A'ishah regarding the verse: "He is the one in want, whose livelihood hardly becomes easy for him."

al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Fatimah bint Qays that she asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this verse, and he said: "Indeed, in wealth there is a right other than the zakat," and he recited this verse: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west…﴾ up to His saying ﴿and [gives wealth] to the slaves, and establishes prayer and gives zakat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾: "the path of defecation and urination."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 51, verse 1–23 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Dhariyat was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿By the winds that scatter dust, scattering﴾. It is said: dharat al-rih al-turab tadhruhu dharwan (the wind scattered the dust), and adhrat tudhriihi dharyan. He, glorified is He, swore by the winds that scatter the dust. The accusative of "dharwan" is as a verbal noun (masdar), and the governing element in it is the active participle, while the object is omitted.

Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read the "ta'" of (al-Dhariyat) as assimilated into the "dhal" of (dharwan). The rest read without assimilation.

It was said: the one sworn by is implied, and it is the Lord of the winds and what follows them; but the first (view) is more preferable.

﴿And by those that bear a load﴾. They are the clouds, which carry water as the four-legged animals carry a load. The accusative of (wiqran) is as its being an object, as it is said: "So-and-so carried a heavy bag." The majority read (wiqran) with a kasra on the waw, as the name of what is carried, i.e., what is borne. It was read with a fatha on it, as a verbal noun, with the governing element being the active participle, or by calling the carried thing by the verbal noun for emphasis.

﴿And by those that glide with ease﴾. They are the ships that run on the sea with the winds, gliding easily.

The accusative of (yusran) is as a verbal noun, or an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or as a circumstantial state: i.e., gliding with ease.

It was said: they are the winds. It was said: the clouds. The first is more preferable.

Al-yusr: ease in everything.

﴿And by those that distribute by command﴾. They are the angels who distribute the affairs.

Al-Farra' said: they bring different commands: Jibril with severity, Mika'il with mercy, and the Angel of Death brings death. It was said: they bring different commands of drought, fertility, rain, death, and events.

It was said: they are the clouds through which Allah distributes the affairs of His servants. It was said: the intended meaning of the dhariyat, the hamilat, the jariyat, and the muqassimat is the winds, for they are described by all of that: they scatter dust, carry clouds, run through the air, and distribute rains. But this is very weak.

The accusative of (amran) is as the object; it was said: as a state, i.e., commanded. The first is more preferable.

﴿Indeed what you are promised is true﴾. This is the answer to the oath: i.e., what you are promised of reward and punishment will certainly come about.

(Ma) may be a relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun, or a verbal (masdariyya) particle.

The reason for singling out these matters for oaths is that they are wondrous matters contrary to the usual course; so whoever is able to do these is able to resurrect, which is what is promised.

﴿And by the heaven with its paths﴾. The majority read (al-hubuk) with a damma on the ha' and the ba'. It was read with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the ba', and with a kasra on the ha' and a fatha on the ba', and with a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the ba'.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: these are dialects. The intended "heaven" here is the well-known one. It was said: the intended meaning is the clouds; but the first is more preferable.

The commentators differed in the interpretation of (al-hubuk). Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said: the meaning is "possessing a well-proportioned, beautiful creation."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: everything you have made firm and done well, you have "habakta" and "ihtabakta" it.

al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "possessing adornment."

It is also narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "possessing stars."

al-Dahhak said: "possessing paths," and al-Farra' said likewise. It is said of what you see in water and sand when the wind touches it: hubuk.

Al-Farra' said: al-hibk with a kasra: everything like sand when still wind passes over it, and water when wind passes over it. A coat of iron is also called hubuk, and from it is the poet's saying:

"As if the weavers had draped it with a carpet, in whose weaving are hibak (lines)."

i.e., paths.

It was said: al-habk means strength, and the meaning is: "and by the heaven possessing strength." A firmly made one (mahbuk) is a strongly created one, of a horse or other, and from it is the poet's saying:

"He has begun to carry me on his nose, a swift one with firm flanks, well-built and firmly made."

Another said:

"Religion has become disordered, so I prepared for it one with a high withers and a firmly knit shoulder-blade."

Al-Wahidi, after relating the first opinion, said: this is the view of most of them.

﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. This is the answer to the oath by the heaven possessing paths: i.e., indeed you, O people of Makkah, are in a discordant, contradictory saying about Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace: some of you say he is a poet, some of you say he is a sorcerer, and some of you say he is a madman.

The reason for specifying the oath by the heaven described by that attribute is the comparison of their sayings in their divergence to the divergence of the heaven's paths. The use of hubuk for paths is what the lexicographers hold, although most commentators differ from it.

Moreover, those sayings about the interpretation of hubuk may return to this, by saying that what is in the heaven of paths may be a cause of greater beauty, evenness of creation, the existence of adornment in it, and greater strength for it.

It was said: the intended meaning of their being "in a discordant saying" is that some of them deny the Resurrection and some doubt it. It was said: their acknowledging that Allah is their Creator while worshipping idols.

﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾. That is: he is turned away from belief in the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and from what he brought, or from the truth, which is the Resurrection and monotheism, whoever is turned away.

It was said: whoever Allah has turned away from that discord by protection and success is turned away from it. It is said: afakahu yafakuhu ifkan: i.e., he turned him from a thing and diverted him from it, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: have you come to us to turn us away?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22]. Mujahid said: "yu'fan 'anhu man ufin" (he is deprived of sense whoever is deprived of sense); al-afn is corruption of the intellect. It was said: "yuhram-hu man hurim" (he is deprived of it whoever is deprived).

Qutrub said: "yujda' 'anhu man judi'" (he is cut off from it whoever is cut off).

al-Yazidi said: "yudfa' 'anhu man dufi'" (he is repelled from it whoever is repelled).

﴿Slain are the conjecturers﴾. This is a curse upon them.

al-Wahidi related from the commentators all together that the meaning is: "the liars are cursed."

Ibn al-Anbari said: qatl, when reported about Allah, has the meaning of cursing, because whomever Allah curses is like one who has been slain and destroyed.

al-Farra' said: the meaning of qutila is: "cursed."

Al-kharrasun: the liars who guess about what they do not know, so they say: Muhammad is a madman, a liar, a poet, a sorcerer.

al-Zajjaj said: al-kharrasun are the liars, and al-kharS is estimating what is on the palm trees of ripe dates as dates; al-kharrasu is the one who estimates them, and that is not what is meant here.

Then He said: ﴿Who are in heedlessness, inattentive﴾. That is: in negligence and the blindness of ignorance concerning the affairs of the Hereafter. The meaning of (sahun) is: frivolous, heedless. Sahw is negligence of a thing and its departure from the heart. The origin of ghamrah is what covers and overspreads a thing, and from it are the pangs (ghamarat) of death.

﴿They ask: when is the Day of Judgment?﴾. That is: they say when the Day of Recompense is, in denial and mockery.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about that day, saying: ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾. That is: they will be burned and punished. It is said: fatantu al-dhahab: when you burn it to test it, and the origin of fitnah is testing.

'Ikrimah said: Do you not see that when gold is put into fire it is said: it was fatana (tested)?

The accusative of (yawma) is governed by an implied element: i.e., the requital is on the day they are over the Fire. It may be a substitute for (yawm al-din), and the fatha is for construction because it is attached to a clause. It was said: it is accusative by the implied "I mean."

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (yawmu) with a damma as a substitute for (yawm al-din).

The clause ﴿Taste your fitnah﴾ is by implied speech: i.e., it will be said to them: taste your punishment; said by Ibn Zayd. Mujahid said: your burning. al-Farra' preferred the first.

The clause ﴿This is what you used to seek to hasten﴾ is part of what is quoted by the saying: i.e., this is what you used to seek to hasten, in mockery from you. It was said: it is a substitute for "your fitnah".

﴿Indeed the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾. When He, glorified is He, mentioned the state of the people of the Fire, He mentioned the state of the people of Paradise: i.e., they will be in orchards in which there are flowing springs, whose description the describers cannot reach.

﴿Receiving what their Lord has given them﴾. That is: accepting what their Lord has given them of good and honor. The clause ﴿Indeed they were before that doers of good﴾ is a reason for what precedes it: i.e., because they were in the world doers of good in their righteous deeds, by doing what they were commanded and abandoning what they were forbidden.

Then He explained their goodness, which He described them with, saying: ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾. Al-huju': sleep at night, not by day. The meaning: they used to sleep little of the night. (Ma) is superfluous, and it may be a verbal (masdariyya) particle or a relative pronoun: i.e., they were little of the night in their sleep, or in what they slept. From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"The helmet has pressed upon my head, so I do not taste sleep except a light doze."

Al-tuhja': a little of sleep. From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

"Does the caller and the hearer of Rayhanah stir me, and my companions in slumber?"

It was said: (ma) is negative, i.e., they did not sleep a little of the night, let alone much of it; and this is very weak.

This is the view of those who say the meaning is that their number was small.

Then He began: ﴿They sleep not﴾, and Ibn al-Anbari said so, and it is weaker than what precedes it.

Qatadah said in the interpretation of this verse: they used to pray between the two evening prayers; Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Wahb said likewise.

﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾. That is: they ask Allah, glorified is He, in the times of dawn to forgive their sins.

al-Hasan said: they extended the prayer to the dawns, then took up seeking forgiveness at the dawns.

al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Mujahid said: they pray at the dawns, because their prayer is a request from them for forgiveness.

al-Dahhak said: it is the Fajr prayer.

Then He mentioned their charities, saying: ﴿And in their wealth is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾. That is: they place in their wealth, on themselves, a right for the beggar and the deprived, seeking nearness to Allah, mighty and majestic.

Muhammad ibn Sirin and Qatadah said: the right here is the obligatory zakah. The first is more preferable, so it is taken to mean voluntary charity, the maintenance of kinship, and hospitality to guests, because the surah is Meccan, and zakah was not made obligatory except in Madinah. It will come in Surat Sa'ala Sa'il: ﴿In their wealth is a known right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 24–25], with the addition of "known." The beggar is the one who asks people because of his poverty.

It is differed concerning the interpretation of the deprived. It was said: he is the one who abstains from asking until people think him rich, so they do not give to him; this is the view of Qatadah and al-Zuhri.

al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: he is the one who has no share in the spoils and from whom nothing from the fay' is paid. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is the one whose fruit, crop or livestock has been struck. al-Qurtubi said: he is the one whom a calamity has struck. It was said: he who does not earn; it was said: he who does not find a sufficiency to suffice him; it was said: he who seeks the world and it turns away from him; it was said: he is the owned one; it was said: the dog; it was said: other than that.

al-Sha'bi said: For me today there are seventy years since I reached puberty, asking about the deprived, and I am today no more knowledgeable about it than I was then. What should be relied upon is what the linguistic meaning indicates: al-mahrum in the language is the prevented, from hirman, which is prevention. It therefore includes whoever is deprived of provision from the root, whoever has had his wealth struck by a calamity that destroyed it, whoever is deprived of a gift, and whoever is deprived of charity because of his abstinence.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the signs He has set up, indicating His oneness and the truth of His promise and threat, saying: ﴿And in the earth are signs for the certain﴾. That is: clear proofs and manifest indications, from the mountains, the land, the sea, the trees, the rivers, and the fruits; and in them are traces of destruction for the disbelieving nations who denied what the messengers of Allah brought and called them to. He singled out those certain of Allah because they are the ones who acknowledge that and reflect upon it, so they benefit from it.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 51, verses 1–23 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ That is: in yourselves there are signs that point to the Oneness of Allah and to the truth of what the messengers brought. He created them as a drop (*nutfah*), then a clinging clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then bones, until He breathes the spirit (*ruh*) into them. After that their forms, colours, natures and tongues differ. Then the very creation of them in this wondrous state, of flesh, blood, bone, limbs, senses, passages, and channels, is itself a sign. The meaning of ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ is: will you not look with the eye of insight, so that you may infer from this the Creator, the Provider, who alone is worthy of divinity, that He has no partner, no equal and no rival, that His promise is true, that His word is true, and that what His messengers have brought you is the truth about which there is no doubt and against which no doubt can prevail. It has also been said that by "the selves" (*anfus*) is meant the spirits (*arwah*), that is: in your souls, through which you live, there are signs.

﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾: that is, the cause of your provision, which is rain, for it is the cause of sustenance.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: "Provision here means what descends from the heaven, of rain and snow."

It has also been said that by "the heaven" is meant the clouds, that is: in the clouds is your provision. It has been said that by "the heaven" is meant rain, and it was called "heaven" because it descends from its direction. From this is the saying of the poet:

*When the sky descends upon the land of a people,*
*we graze upon it, even if they are angry.*

Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning is "and upon the Lord of the heaven is your provision," and a parallel to this is ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud: 6], but this is far-fetched.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: that is, with Allah in the heaven is your provision.

It has also been said that the meaning is: in the heaven is the decree of your provision.

The majority read *rizqukum* in the singular, while Ya'qub, Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read *arzaqukum* in the plural.

﴿And what you are promised﴾: of Paradise and Hellfire, as said by Mujahid. 'Ata' said: of reward and punishment. al-Kalbi said: of good and evil. Ibn Sirin said: what you are promised of the matter of the Hour. al-Rabi' also said this.

The preferable reading is to take it in the sense that is more general than all these opinions, for the recompense of deeds is written in the heaven, the decree and destiny descend from it, and Paradise and Hellfire are in it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, swore by Himself, saying: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾, that is, what I inform you of in these verses.

al-Zajjaj said: it is what He mentioned of the matter of provision and the signs.

al-Kalbi said: it means what was related in the Book.

Muqatil said: it means the matter of the Hour.

It has also been said that *ma* in His saying ﴿and what you are promised﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾, so the pronoun refers back to *ma*.

Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿like that you speak﴾. The majority read *mithla* with the accusative (*nasb*), on the presumption of "like your speech", with *ma* being superfluous (*za'idah*). Some of the Kufans said this, that it is accusative by the removal of the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*).

al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: it may be in the accusative as an emphatic (*tawkid*), that is: it is truly true, like your speech.

al-Mazini said: *mithl* together with *ma* has the status of a single word, and so it is built on the fatha.

Sibawayh said: it is indeclinable (*mabni*) because it is annexed to something that is not fully declinable. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and al-A'mash read *mithlu* with the nominative, as an adjective (*sifah*) of *haqq*, because *mithl* is indefinite, and even when annexed it does not become definite, like *ghayr*.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the view of al-Mazini, and said: a similar example is the saying of Humayd:

*Woe to whoever does not know what they are, woe indeed!*

Here *waylan* is built with *ma* and is not given tanwin. The meaning of the verse is a comparison of the certainty of what Allah has informed about with the certainty of human speech and existence. This is like your saying: "it is true, as you are here", and "it is true, as you are speaking." The meaning is that it is true in its truthfulness and existence, as what you know by necessity.

[p. 1406]

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, from various chains, transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His saying ﴿By those that scatter with dispersal﴾: "the winds." ﴿And those that carry a load﴾: "the clouds." ﴿And those that glide with ease﴾: "the ships." ﴿And those that distribute by command﴾: "the angels."

al-Bazzar, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab the like of this, and traced it back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In its chain is Abu Bakr ibn Sabrah, who is weak in narration (*layyin al-hadith*), and Sa'id ibn Sallam, who is not among the people of hadith. So said al-Bazzar.

Ibn Kathir said: this hadith is weak in its attribution to the Prophet, and the closest thing to it is that it is a statement of 'Umar (*mawquf*).

al-Firyabi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas the like of the statement of 'Ali.

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿By the heaven of the intricate paths﴾: "its beauty and its evenness."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* transmitted from him regarding the verse: "possessing splendour and beauty, and its construction is like the hail, interlocked."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar the like of this.

Ibn Mani' transmitted from 'Ali: "it is the seventh heaven."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾: "It is led astray from it, whoever is led astray."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also ﴿Destroyed are the liars﴾: "Cursed are the doubters."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "They are the soothsayers." ﴿Who are in heedlessness, inattentive﴾: "in negligence, playing."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "Heedlessness (*ghamrah*) is disbelief and doubt."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "In their misguidance they keep wandering." And regarding His saying ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾: "they will be punished."

These same transmitters also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Taking what their Lord has given them﴾: "the obligations (*fara'id*)." ﴿Indeed they were before that doers of good﴾: "before the obligations were revealed, they used to act."

These, together with al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat*, transmitted from him also regarding ﴿They used to sleep little of the night﴾: "there was not a night that came upon them in which they slept until morning, except that they prayed during it."

Ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also regarding the verse: "they used to sleep only little."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, transmitted from Anas regarding the verse: "they used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha'."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar regarding ﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾: "they pray."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾: "other than the zakat, by which one maintains kinship, or hosts a guest, or helps a deprived person."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "The beggar (*sa'il*) is the one who asks people, and the deprived (*mahrum*) is the one who has no share of the spoils (*fay'*) of the Muslims."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "The deprived is the one who is in want (*muharif*), who seeks the world and it turns away from him, and who does not ask people. So Allah commanded the believers to support him."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'A'ishah regarding the verse: "He is the one in want, whose livelihood hardly becomes easy for him."

al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Fatimah bint Qays that she asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this verse, and he said: "Indeed, in wealth there is a right other than the zakat," and he recited this verse: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west…﴾ up to His saying ﴿and [gives wealth] to the slaves, and establishes prayer and gives zakat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾: "the path of defecation and urination."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 51, verse 1–23 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Dhariyat was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿By the winds that scatter dust, scattering﴾. It is said: dharat al-rih al-turab tadhruhu dharwan (the wind scattered the dust), and adhrat tudhriihi dharyan. He, glorified is He, swore by the winds that scatter the dust. The accusative of "dharwan" is as a verbal noun (masdar), and the governing element in it is the active participle, while the object is omitted.

Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read the "ta'" of (al-Dhariyat) as assimilated into the "dhal" of (dharwan). The rest read without assimilation.

It was said: the one sworn by is implied, and it is the Lord of the winds and what follows them; but the first (view) is more preferable.

﴿And by those that bear a load﴾. They are the clouds, which carry water as the four-legged animals carry a load. The accusative of (wiqran) is as its being an object, as it is said: "So-and-so carried a heavy bag." The majority read (wiqran) with a kasra on the waw, as the name of what is carried, i.e., what is borne. It was read with a fatha on it, as a verbal noun, with the governing element being the active participle, or by calling the carried thing by the verbal noun for emphasis.

﴿And by those that glide with ease﴾. They are the ships that run on the sea with the winds, gliding easily.

The accusative of (yusran) is as a verbal noun, or an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or as a circumstantial state: i.e., gliding with ease.

It was said: they are the winds. It was said: the clouds. The first is more preferable.

Al-yusr: ease in everything.

﴿And by those that distribute by command﴾. They are the angels who distribute the affairs.

Al-Farra' said: they bring different commands: Jibril with severity, Mika'il with mercy, and the Angel of Death brings death. It was said: they bring different commands of drought, fertility, rain, death, and events.

It was said: they are the clouds through which Allah distributes the affairs of His servants. It was said: the intended meaning of the dhariyat, the hamilat, the jariyat, and the muqassimat is the winds, for they are described by all of that: they scatter dust, carry clouds, run through the air, and distribute rains. But this is very weak.

The accusative of (amran) is as the object; it was said: as a state, i.e., commanded. The first is more preferable.

﴿Indeed what you are promised is true﴾. This is the answer to the oath: i.e., what you are promised of reward and punishment will certainly come about.

(Ma) may be a relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun, or a verbal (masdariyya) particle.

The reason for singling out these matters for oaths is that they are wondrous matters contrary to the usual course; so whoever is able to do these is able to resurrect, which is what is promised.

﴿And by the heaven with its paths﴾. The majority read (al-hubuk) with a damma on the ha' and the ba'. It was read with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the ba', and with a kasra on the ha' and a fatha on the ba', and with a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the ba'.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: these are dialects. The intended "heaven" here is the well-known one. It was said: the intended meaning is the clouds; but the first is more preferable.

The commentators differed in the interpretation of (al-hubuk). Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said: the meaning is "possessing a well-proportioned, beautiful creation."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: everything you have made firm and done well, you have "habakta" and "ihtabakta" it.

al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "possessing adornment."

It is also narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "possessing stars."

al-Dahhak said: "possessing paths," and al-Farra' said likewise. It is said of what you see in water and sand when the wind touches it: hubuk.

Al-Farra' said: al-hibk with a kasra: everything like sand when still wind passes over it, and water when wind passes over it. A coat of iron is also called hubuk, and from it is the poet's saying:

"As if the weavers had draped it with a carpet, in whose weaving are hibak (lines)."

i.e., paths.

It was said: al-habk means strength, and the meaning is: "and by the heaven possessing strength." A firmly made one (mahbuk) is a strongly created one, of a horse or other, and from it is the poet's saying:

"He has begun to carry me on his nose, a swift one with firm flanks, well-built and firmly made."

Another said:

"Religion has become disordered, so I prepared for it one with a high withers and a firmly knit shoulder-blade."

Al-Wahidi, after relating the first opinion, said: this is the view of most of them.

﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾. This is the answer to the oath by the heaven possessing paths: i.e., indeed you, O people of Makkah, are in a discordant, contradictory saying about Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace: some of you say he is a poet, some of you say he is a sorcerer, and some of you say he is a madman.

The reason for specifying the oath by the heaven described by that attribute is the comparison of their sayings in their divergence to the divergence of the heaven's paths. The use of hubuk for paths is what the lexicographers hold, although most commentators differ from it.

Moreover, those sayings about the interpretation of hubuk may return to this, by saying that what is in the heaven of paths may be a cause of greater beauty, evenness of creation, the existence of adornment in it, and greater strength for it.

It was said: the intended meaning of their being "in a discordant saying" is that some of them deny the Resurrection and some doubt it. It was said: their acknowledging that Allah is their Creator while worshipping idols.

﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾. That is: he is turned away from belief in the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and from what he brought, or from the truth, which is the Resurrection and monotheism, whoever is turned away.

It was said: whoever Allah has turned away from that discord by protection and success is turned away from it. It is said: afakahu yafakuhu ifkan: i.e., he turned him from a thing and diverted him from it, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: have you come to us to turn us away?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22]. Mujahid said: "yu'fan 'anhu man ufin" (he is deprived of sense whoever is deprived of sense); al-afn is corruption of the intellect. It was said: "yuhram-hu man hurim" (he is deprived of it whoever is deprived).

Qutrub said: "yujda' 'anhu man judi'" (he is cut off from it whoever is cut off).

al-Yazidi said: "yudfa' 'anhu man dufi'" (he is repelled from it whoever is repelled).

﴿Slain are the conjecturers﴾. This is a curse upon them.

al-Wahidi related from the commentators all together that the meaning is: "the liars are cursed."

Ibn al-Anbari said: qatl, when reported about Allah, has the meaning of cursing, because whomever Allah curses is like one who has been slain and destroyed.

al-Farra' said: the meaning of qutila is: "cursed."

Al-kharrasun: the liars who guess about what they do not know, so they say: Muhammad is a madman, a liar, a poet, a sorcerer.

al-Zajjaj said: al-kharrasun are the liars, and al-kharS is estimating what is on the palm trees of ripe dates as dates; al-kharrasu is the one who estimates them, and that is not what is meant here.

Then He said: ﴿Who are in heedlessness, inattentive﴾. That is: in negligence and the blindness of ignorance concerning the affairs of the Hereafter. The meaning of (sahun) is: frivolous, heedless. Sahw is negligence of a thing and its departure from the heart. The origin of ghamrah is what covers and overspreads a thing, and from it are the pangs (ghamarat) of death.

﴿They ask: when is the Day of Judgment?﴾. That is: they say when the Day of Recompense is, in denial and mockery.

Then He, glorified is He, informed about that day, saying: ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾. That is: they will be burned and punished. It is said: fatantu al-dhahab: when you burn it to test it, and the origin of fitnah is testing.

'Ikrimah said: Do you not see that when gold is put into fire it is said: it was fatana (tested)?

The accusative of (yawma) is governed by an implied element: i.e., the requital is on the day they are over the Fire. It may be a substitute for (yawm al-din), and the fatha is for construction because it is attached to a clause. It was said: it is accusative by the implied "I mean."

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (yawmu) with a damma as a substitute for (yawm al-din).

The clause ﴿Taste your fitnah﴾ is by implied speech: i.e., it will be said to them: taste your punishment; said by Ibn Zayd. Mujahid said: your burning. al-Farra' preferred the first.

The clause ﴿This is what you used to seek to hasten﴾ is part of what is quoted by the saying: i.e., this is what you used to seek to hasten, in mockery from you. It was said: it is a substitute for "your fitnah".

﴿Indeed the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾. When He, glorified is He, mentioned the state of the people of the Fire, He mentioned the state of the people of Paradise: i.e., they will be in orchards in which there are flowing springs, whose description the describers cannot reach.

﴿Receiving what their Lord has given them﴾. That is: accepting what their Lord has given them of good and honor. The clause ﴿Indeed they were before that doers of good﴾ is a reason for what precedes it: i.e., because they were in the world doers of good in their righteous deeds, by doing what they were commanded and abandoning what they were forbidden.

Then He explained their goodness, which He described them with, saying: ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾. Al-huju': sleep at night, not by day. The meaning: they used to sleep little of the night. (Ma) is superfluous, and it may be a verbal (masdariyya) particle or a relative pronoun: i.e., they were little of the night in their sleep, or in what they slept. From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"The helmet has pressed upon my head, so I do not taste sleep except a light doze."

Al-tuhja': a little of sleep. From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

"Does the caller and the hearer of Rayhanah stir me, and my companions in slumber?"

It was said: (ma) is negative, i.e., they did not sleep a little of the night, let alone much of it; and this is very weak.

This is the view of those who say the meaning is that their number was small.

Then He began: ﴿They sleep not﴾, and Ibn al-Anbari said so, and it is weaker than what precedes it.

Qatadah said in the interpretation of this verse: they used to pray between the two evening prayers; Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Wahb said likewise.

﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾. That is: they ask Allah, glorified is He, in the times of dawn to forgive their sins.

al-Hasan said: they extended the prayer to the dawns, then took up seeking forgiveness at the dawns.

al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Mujahid said: they pray at the dawns, because their prayer is a request from them for forgiveness.

al-Dahhak said: it is the Fajr prayer.

Then He mentioned their charities, saying: ﴿And in their wealth is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾. That is: they place in their wealth, on themselves, a right for the beggar and the deprived, seeking nearness to Allah, mighty and majestic.

Muhammad ibn Sirin and Qatadah said: the right here is the obligatory zakah. The first is more preferable, so it is taken to mean voluntary charity, the maintenance of kinship, and hospitality to guests, because the surah is Meccan, and zakah was not made obligatory except in Madinah. It will come in Surat Sa'ala Sa'il: ﴿In their wealth is a known right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 24–25], with the addition of "known." The beggar is the one who asks people because of his poverty.

It is differed concerning the interpretation of the deprived. It was said: he is the one who abstains from asking until people think him rich, so they do not give to him; this is the view of Qatadah and al-Zuhri.

al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: he is the one who has no share in the spoils and from whom nothing from the fay' is paid. Zayd ibn Aslam said: he is the one whose fruit, crop or livestock has been struck. al-Qurtubi said: he is the one whom a calamity has struck. It was said: he who does not earn; it was said: he who does not find a sufficiency to suffice him; it was said: he who seeks the world and it turns away from him; it was said: he is the owned one; it was said: the dog; it was said: other than that.

al-Sha'bi said: For me today there are seventy years since I reached puberty, asking about the deprived, and I am today no more knowledgeable about it than I was then. What should be relied upon is what the linguistic meaning indicates: al-mahrum in the language is the prevented, from hirman, which is prevention. It therefore includes whoever is deprived of provision from the root, whoever has had his wealth struck by a calamity that destroyed it, whoever is deprived of a gift, and whoever is deprived of charity because of his abstinence.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the signs He has set up, indicating His oneness and the truth of His promise and threat, saying: ﴿And in the earth are signs for the certain﴾. That is: clear proofs and manifest indications, from the mountains, the land, the sea, the trees, the rivers, and the fruits; and in them are traces of destruction for the disbelieving nations who denied what the messengers of Allah brought and called them to. He singled out those certain of Allah because they are the ones who acknowledge that and reflect upon it, so they benefit from it.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 51, verses 1–23 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾ That is: in yourselves there are signs that point to the Oneness of Allah and to the truth of what the messengers brought. He created them as a drop (*nutfah*), then a clinging clot (*'alaqah*), then a lump of flesh (*mudghah*), then bones, until He breathes the spirit (*ruh*) into them. After that their forms, colours, natures and tongues differ. Then the very creation of them in this wondrous state, of flesh, blood, bone, limbs, senses, passages, and channels, is itself a sign. The meaning of ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ is: will you not look with the eye of insight, so that you may infer from this the Creator, the Provider, who alone is worthy of divinity, that He has no partner, no equal and no rival, that His promise is true, that His word is true, and that what His messengers have brought you is the truth about which there is no doubt and against which no doubt can prevail. It has also been said that by "the selves" (*anfus*) is meant the spirits (*arwah*), that is: in your souls, through which you live, there are signs.

﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾: that is, the cause of your provision, which is rain, for it is the cause of sustenance.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: "Provision here means what descends from the heaven, of rain and snow."

It has also been said that by "the heaven" is meant the clouds, that is: in the clouds is your provision. It has been said that by "the heaven" is meant rain, and it was called "heaven" because it descends from its direction. From this is the saying of the poet:

*When the sky descends upon the land of a people,*
*we graze upon it, even if they are angry.*

Ibn Kaysan said: the meaning is "and upon the Lord of the heaven is your provision," and a parallel to this is ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud: 6], but this is far-fetched.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: that is, with Allah in the heaven is your provision.

It has also been said that the meaning is: in the heaven is the decree of your provision.

The majority read *rizqukum* in the singular, while Ya'qub, Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read *arzaqukum* in the plural.

﴿And what you are promised﴾: of Paradise and Hellfire, as said by Mujahid. 'Ata' said: of reward and punishment. al-Kalbi said: of good and evil. Ibn Sirin said: what you are promised of the matter of the Hour. al-Rabi' also said this.

The preferable reading is to take it in the sense that is more general than all these opinions, for the recompense of deeds is written in the heaven, the decree and destiny descend from it, and Paradise and Hellfire are in it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, swore by Himself, saying: ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾, that is, what I inform you of in these verses.

al-Zajjaj said: it is what He mentioned of the matter of provision and the signs.

al-Kalbi said: it means what was related in the Book.

Muqatil said: it means the matter of the Hour.

It has also been said that *ma* in His saying ﴿and what you are promised﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is ﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾, so the pronoun refers back to *ma*.

Then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿like that you speak﴾. The majority read *mithla* with the accusative (*nasb*), on the presumption of "like your speech", with *ma* being superfluous (*za'idah*). Some of the Kufans said this, that it is accusative by the removal of the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*).

al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' said: it may be in the accusative as an emphatic (*tawkid*), that is: it is truly true, like your speech.

al-Mazini said: *mithl* together with *ma* has the status of a single word, and so it is built on the fatha.

Sibawayh said: it is indeclinable (*mabni*) because it is annexed to something that is not fully declinable. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this reading.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and al-A'mash read *mithlu* with the nominative, as an adjective (*sifah*) of *haqq*, because *mithl* is indefinite, and even when annexed it does not become definite, like *ghayr*.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi preferred the view of al-Mazini, and said: a similar example is the saying of Humayd:

*Woe to whoever does not know what they are, woe indeed!*

Here *waylan* is built with *ma* and is not given tanwin. The meaning of the verse is a comparison of the certainty of what Allah has informed about with the certainty of human speech and existence. This is like your saying: "it is true, as you are here", and "it is true, as you are speaking." The meaning is that it is true in its truthfulness and existence, as what you know by necessity.

[p. 1406]

Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, from various chains, transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His saying ﴿By those that scatter with dispersal﴾: "the winds." ﴿And those that carry a load﴾: "the clouds." ﴿And those that glide with ease﴾: "the ships." ﴿And those that distribute by command﴾: "the angels."

al-Bazzar, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab the like of this, and traced it back to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In its chain is Abu Bakr ibn Sabrah, who is weak in narration (*layyin al-hadith*), and Sa'id ibn Sallam, who is not among the people of hadith. So said al-Bazzar.

Ibn Kathir said: this hadith is weak in its attribution to the Prophet, and the closest thing to it is that it is a statement of 'Umar (*mawquf*).

al-Firyabi and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas the like of the statement of 'Ali.

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿By the heaven of the intricate paths﴾: "its beauty and its evenness."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azamah* transmitted from him regarding the verse: "possessing splendour and beauty, and its construction is like the hail, interlocked."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar the like of this.

Ibn Mani' transmitted from 'Ali: "it is the seventh heaven."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾: "It is led astray from it, whoever is led astray."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also ﴿Destroyed are the liars﴾: "Cursed are the doubters."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "They are the soothsayers." ﴿Who are in heedlessness, inattentive﴾: "in negligence, playing."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "Heedlessness (*ghamrah*) is disbelief and doubt."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "In their misguidance they keep wandering." And regarding His saying ﴿The Day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾: "they will be punished."

These same transmitters also transmitted from him regarding His saying ﴿Taking what their Lord has given them﴾: "the obligations (*fara'id*)." ﴿Indeed they were before that doers of good﴾: "before the obligations were revealed, they used to act."

These, together with al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat*, transmitted from him also regarding ﴿They used to sleep little of the night﴾: "there was not a night that came upon them in which they slept until morning, except that they prayed during it."

Ibn Nasr, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also regarding the verse: "they used to sleep only little."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, transmitted from Anas regarding the verse: "they used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha'."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Umar regarding ﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾: "they pray."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾: "other than the zakat, by which one maintains kinship, or hosts a guest, or helps a deprived person."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him: "The beggar (*sa'il*) is the one who asks people, and the deprived (*mahrum*) is the one who has no share of the spoils (*fay'*) of the Muslims."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also: "The deprived is the one who is in want (*muharif*), who seeks the world and it turns away from him, and who does not ask people. So Allah commanded the believers to support him."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from 'A'ishah regarding the verse: "He is the one in want, whose livelihood hardly becomes easy for him."

al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* transmitted from Fatimah bint Qays that she asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this verse, and he said: "Indeed, in wealth there is a right other than the zakat," and he recited this verse: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west…﴾ up to His saying ﴿and [gives wealth] to the slaves, and establishes prayer and gives zakat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177].

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿And in yourselves. Will you not then see?﴾: "the path of defecation and urination."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 51, verse 1–23 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Dhariyat was revealed in Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿By the winds that scatter dust, scattering﴾. It is said: dharat al-rih al-turab tadhruhu dharwan (the wind scattered the dust), and adhrat tudhriihi dharyan. He, glorified is He, swore by the winds that scatter the dust. The accusative of "dharwan" is as a verbal noun (masdar), and the governing element in it is the active participle, while the object is omitted.

Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read the "ta'" of (al-Dhariyat) as assimilated into the "dhal" of (dharwan). The rest read without assimilation.

It was said: the one sworn by is implied, and it is the Lord of the winds and what follows them; but the first (view) is more preferable.

﴿And by those that bear a load﴾. They are the clouds, which carry water as the four-legged animals carry a load. The accusative of (wiqran) is as its being an object, as it is said: "So-and-so carried a heavy bag." The majority read (wiqran) with a kasra on the waw, as the name of what is carried, i.e., what is borne. It was read with a fatha on it, as a verbal noun, with the governing element being the active participle, or by calling the carried thing by the verbal noun for emphasis.

﴿And by those that glide with ease﴾. They are the ships that run on the sea with the winds, gliding easily.

The accusative of (yusran) is as a verbal noun, or an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or as a circumstantial state: i.e., gliding with ease.

It was said: they are the winds. It was said: the clouds. The first is more preferable.

Al-yusr: ease in everything.

﴿And by those that distribute by command﴾. They are the angels who distribute the affairs.

Al-Farra' said: they bring different commands: Jibril with severity, Mika'il with mercy, and the Angel of Death brings death. It was said: they bring different commands of drought, fertility, rain, death, and events.

It was said: they are the clouds through which Allah distributes the affairs of His servants. It was said: the intended meaning of the dhariyat, the hamilat, the jariyat, and the muqassimat is the winds, for they are described by all of that: they scatter dust, carry clouds, run through the air, and distribute rains. But this is very weak.

The accusative of (amran) is as the object; it was said: as a state, i.e., commanded. The first is more preferable.

﴿Indeed what you are promised is true﴾. This is the answer to the oath: i.e., what you are promised of reward and punishment will certainly come about.

(Ma) may be a relative pronoun with an omitted returning pronoun, or a verbal (masdariyya) particle.

The reason for singling out these matters for oaths is that they are wondrous matters contrary to the usual course; so whoever is able to do these is able to resurrect, which is what is promised.

﴿And by the heaven with its paths﴾. The majority read (al-hubuk) with a damma on the ha' and the ba'. It was read with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the ba', and with a kasra on the ha' and a fatha on the ba', and with a kasra on the ha' and a damma on the ba'.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: these are dialects. The intended "heaven" here is the well-known one. It was said: the intended meaning is the clouds; but the first is more preferable.

The commentators differed in the interpretation of (al-hubuk). Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said: the meaning is "possessing a well-proportioned, beautiful creation."

Ibn al-A'rabi said: everything you have made firm and done well, you have "habakta" and "ihtabakta" it.

al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "possessing adornment."

It is also narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "possessing stars."

al-Dahhak said: "possessing paths," and al-Farra' said likewise. It is said of what you see in water and sand when the wind touches it: hubuk.

Al-Farra' said: al-hibk with a kasra: everything like sand when still wind passes over it, and water when wind passes over it. A coat of iron is also called hubuk, and from it is the poet's saying:

"As if the weavers had draped it with a carpet, in whose weaving are hibak (lines)."

i.e., paths.

It was said: al-habk means strength, and the meaning is: "and by the heaven possessing strength." A firmly made one (mahbuk) is a strongly created one, of a horse or other, and from it is the poet's saying:

"He has begun to carry me on his nose, a swift one with firm flanks, well-built and firmly made."

Another said:

"Religion has become disordered, so I prepared for it one with a high withers and a firmly knit shoulder-blade."

Al-Wahidi, after relating the first opinion, said: this is the view of most of them.

﴿Indeed you are in a discordant saying﴾.
